Organization of the Periodic Table: The modern periodic table orders the elements by increasing atomic number, a correction Moseley made to Mendeleev's mass-based table of 1869. The periodic law states that properties repeat periodically with atomic number. Rows are periods (7) and columns are groups (18). The table divides into s, p, d and f blocks according to the sublevel being filled, and period lengths are 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 and 32. Dobereiner's triads and Mendeleev's predicted gaps were early steps toward this pattern.
Groups, Periods and Families: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, so they behave alike chemically, while the period number gives the highest occupied energy level. Key families are the alkali metals (group 1), alkaline earth metals (group 2), halogens (group 17) and noble gases (group 18). Metals lose valence electrons and nonmetals gain them to reach a noble gas configuration. Compound formulas come from balancing charges, so calcium and chlorine give CaCl2, and aluminum and oxygen give Al2O3.
Periodic Trends in Atomic Radius: Atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of bonded identical atoms. It increases down a group because each period adds an energy level and inner electrons shield the outer ones. It decreases across a period because the effective nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same level. Cations are smaller than their atoms, anions are larger, and among isoelectronic ions the one with more protons is smaller.
Ionization Energy and Electronegativity: First ionization energy is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom. It increases across a period and decreases down a group, and successive ionization energies rise, with a large jump once an inner level is reached. Electronegativity is an atom's ability to attract bonding electrons and follows the same trend, with fluorine highest at 4.0. An electronegativity difference above about 1.7 gives an ionic bond, 0.5 to 1.7 polar covalent, and below 0.5 nonpolar covalent.
Metals, Nonmetals and Metalloids: A stair-step line separates metals on the left from nonmetals on the right, with metalloids along the line. Metals are shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors, and they form cations with basic oxides. Nonmetals are dull, brittle and poor conductors, and they form acidic oxides. Metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) are semiconductors with mixed properties. Alloys such as brass and steel are mixtures of metals, and metallic bonding with free valence electrons explains conductivity and malleability.
